pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 5–6 years

- **Topic:** Describing Material Properties

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS1 Y1 'Everyday materials'):** Pupils should be taught to "describe the simple physical properties of a variety of everyday materials." Non-statutory guidance lists the target property vocabulary as "hard/soft; stretchy/stiff; shiny/dull; rough/smooth; bendy/not bendy; waterproof/not waterproof; absorbent/not absorbent; opaque/transparent," learned as pupils "explore and experiment with a wide variety of materials."

- **Standards — US (NGSS 2-PS1-1):** "[curriculum wording omitted; reference 2-PS1-1]." The clarification statement names "[curriculum wording omitted; reference 2-PS1-1]." DCI PS1.A: "[curriculum wording omitted; reference 2-PS1-1]." SEP: Planning and Carrying Out Investigations; CCC: Patterns.

- **Operational details:** Teach each property as a paired opposite (hard/soft, shiny/dull, rough/smooth, waterproof/absorbent, transparent/opaque) attached to a testable observation. Give children real materials to feel, bend, and test: run a finger over rough brick vs smooth glass, try to stretch elastic vs stiff wood, drip water onto a paper towel (absorbent) vs a plastic sheet (waterproof), hold materials to the light (transparent vs opaque). Insist that describing means using the property WORD tied to what was observed, and push the 'why it matters' link (waterproof = water doesn't soak through). The DfE working-scientifically exemplar 'What is the best material for an umbrella?' is the natural culminating fair test.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A (concrete/observational). The child can use at least five property words correctly, describe three materials with two property words each, and explain why one property matters (e.g. 'waterproof means the rain stays out') — showing the vocabulary is anchored to observed behaviour, not guessed from appearance.
bestPractices: Teach properties as testable opposite-pairs (waterproof/absorbent, transparent/opaque) so each word has a clear contrast and a simple test.
Ground every property word in a hands-on test the child performs — feel, bend, stretch, drip water, hold to light — rather than reading definitions.
Separate a property from its material's appearance: test whether something is really waterproof or transparent instead of assuming from how it looks.
Push the functional 'why it matters' link (waterproof means water doesn't get through) so properties connect to real uses — scaffolding the Y2 'suitability for a use' work.
Use the DfE fair-test exemplar ('best material for an umbrella?') to apply property words to a real design question.
Model precise property talk and give sentence frames ('this feels…', 'this lets light…') to build the vocabulary explicitly, since technical terms differ from everyday use.
keyRepresentations: Paired-opposite property cards (hard/soft, shiny/dull, rough/smooth, waterproof/absorbent, transparent/opaque)
A materials test bench with simple tests: a light to hold materials against, a water dropper, a bend/stretch station
A property grid (materials down the side, property words across the top) filled from testing
The 'best material for an umbrella' fair-test setup
Sentence-frame talk cards for describing what was observed
commonMisconceptions: Judging a property from appearance instead of testing it — e.g. assuming clear plastic is glass, or that a shiny thing must be metal.
Treating 'transparent' as 'shiny' or muddling see-through with reflective.
Thinking absorbent and waterproof are the same or unrelated, rather than opposite behaviours toward water.
Believing all of one material shares one property (all plastic is hard, all metal is cold/silver), ignoring variety within a material.
Using property words loosely without tying them to an observation, so 'strong', 'hard' and 'stiff' get used interchangeably.

learn.summary: For 5–6-year-olds describing everyday material properties, teach each property as a testable opposite-pair (waterproof/absorbent, transparent/opaque, hard/soft, rough/smooth, stretchy/stiff, bendy/not bendy, shiny/dull) anchored to a hands-on test the child performs — drip water, bend, stretch, hold to a light, feel. The core objective is that a describing word names an OBSERVED behaviour, not something guessed from appearance. Build the vocabulary through naming scaffolds, then move to real (or realistically simulated) tests so children watch a material respond, and apply the words to a design question such as choosing the best material for an umbrella.

activities.title: Materials test bench: watch the property happen
feedback: If a child names a property before testing, invite the test first: 'Let's drip water and watch — then tell me waterproof or absorbent.'
When the water beads and rolls off, point out: 'The water stayed on top — that's waterproof.' When it soaks in: 'It went inside and the towel got darker — that's absorbent.'
For the torch: 'The light went straight through — transparent. The light stopped — opaque.' Watch the beam where it lands beyond the material, not the bulb.
For stretch versus bend: 'It pulled longer — stretchy. This one curved when you pushed it — bendy. The stick did neither — stiff and not bendy.'
If the umbrella choice is based on looks ('the shiny one'), prompt: 'Which one did the water roll off when we tested it?'
activities.rationale: Grounding each property word in a test the child performs supports the aim, in the English national curriculum for Year 1, that pupils describe the simple physical properties of a variety of everyday materials, and it leads towards the later NGSS Grade 2 expectation to [curriculum wording omitted; reference 2-PS1-1]. A simulated bench where acting on a material shows a live, contrasting response can make the cause–effect visible, but real materials give tactile evidence a screen cannot, so hands-on testing is the primary form where feasible.
sourceClaims: NGSS 2-PS1-1 '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 2-PS1-1]'; clarification names color/texture/hardness/flexibility; DCI PS1.A.

DfE KS1 Y1 statutory requirement: pupils taught to 'describe the simple physical properties of a variety of everyday materials'; non-statutory property vocabulary (hard/soft, waterproof/absorbent, transparent/opaque, etc.); WS exemplar 'best material for an umbrella'.
learnerActions: Set up or use a bench with real materials and simple test tools: a water dropper, a bend/stretch station, and a torch or light source.

Drip the same small amount of water onto a plastic raincoat/sheet and onto a paper towel. Watch the drops bead up and roll off the plastic (waterproof) and soak in and darken the fibres of the towel (absorbent). Say the two property words aloud for what you saw.

Shine the torch beam AT a clear plastic sheet, a piece of tissue, and a wooden block, and look at where the beam lands — do not look back toward the light. Notice the beam passes clearly through the clear sheet (transparent), only some light glows dimly through the tissue (it lets some light through, so it is neither fully transparent nor opaque — sometimes called translucent), and the light is stopped by the wood (opaque). Name what each did.

Try two separate tests: stretch an elastic band (it pulls LONGER when you pull it — stretchy) versus a stiff stick (it does not give — stiff); then bend a bendy strip (it CURVES or folds when you push it — bendy) versus the stiff stick (it will not bend — not bendy). Feel how stretching pulls something longer while bending curves or folds it.
Record each result in a property grid — materials down the side, property words across the top — writing or stamping the word only after you have seen the test.
Finish with the fair-test challenge: 'Which material makes the best umbrella?' Use what you tested to choose and say why.
activities.intendedInsight: A property is a behaviour a material shows when you act on it, so a describing word is something you can test and watch happen — not a guess from how the material looks.

activities.title: Name the property: tap-and-reveal vocabulary scaffold
feedback: Confirm correct pairings: 'Yes — shiny is the opposite of dull; stretchy is the opposite of stiff.'

If a child confuses see-through with reflective, separate them: 'Transparent means light goes through; shiny means it bounces light back. A window can be both, but a mirror is shiny and NOT transparent.'
If a child treats stretchy and bendy as the same, note: 'Stretchy pulls longer; bendy curves or folds — they are different tests.'
When a 'guess then check' prediction is wrong, treat the surprise as the lesson: 'You guessed waterproof — let's see what the water actually did.'
activities.rationale: Pre-readers need the property words modelled and attached to exemplars before they can describe independently; audio and lift-the-flap pairs build vocabulary explicitly, since technical terms differ from everyday use. This builds naming but only asserts properties — it does not let the child test them, so it is a scaffold toward, not a substitute for, the observe-and-describe skill.
sourceClaims: DfE KS1 Y1 statutory requirement: pupils taught to 'describe the simple physical properties of a variety of everyday materials'; non-statutory property vocabulary (hard/soft, waterproof/absorbent, transparent/opaque, etc.); WS exemplar 'best material for an umbrella'.
learnerActions: Explore a scene of familiar materials (sponge, window, brick, elastic band, metal spoon, wooden block).
Tap or point to each one to hear/say one or two property words for it — e.g. sponge: 'soft, absorbent'; window: 'hard, transparent'.
Match opposite-pair cards: shiny↔dull, rough↔smooth, waterproof↔absorbent, transparent↔opaque, stretchy↔stiff, bendy↔not bendy.
Play 'guess then check': predict a material's property, then lift the flap (or run the real test) to see the result.
activities.intendedInsight: Each property word has a clear opposite and attaches to example materials, giving children the vocabulary they will then verify by testing.

activities.title: Sort and match: check the words are secure
feedback: For correct sorts, name the evidence: 'Right — water rolls off the plastic, so it's waterproof.'
If a child sorts by appearance, redirect to the tested behaviour rather than the look.
If soft and absorbent get merged, show the soft-but-waterproof plastic bag as a counter-case.
activities.rationale: Matching and categorisation can check whether the vocabulary is secure, but an illustration is only evocative — it cannot show the actual test, so this format verifies prior learning rather than itself eliciting the observing skill. Keep it to properties the children have already tested.
sourceClaims: DfE KS1 Y1 statutory requirement: pupils taught to 'describe the simple physical properties of a variety of everyday materials'; non-statutory property vocabulary (hard/soft, waterproof/absorbent, transparent/opaque, etc.); WS exemplar 'best material for an umbrella'.
learnerActions: Drag materials into category bins: transparent vs opaque; waterproof vs absorbent.
Match each material to the property word(s) that describe it.
Answer picture-and-audio questions about properties — but only for materials you have already tested.
Separate confusable cases: sort a soft plastic bag (soft but waterproof) and a rough dry sponge (rough but absorbent) so each property is judged on its own.
activities.intendedInsight: Property words are secure when a child applies them correctly across varied examples and keeps distinct properties apart.

activities.title: Predict-then-pour: challenging appearance-based judgements
feedback: If the child picks the shiny fabric because it 'looks smart', pour the water and let the surprise result teach: 'It looked right but the water soaked through — what does that tell us?'
If the child says 'all plastic is hard', hand them the soft bendy bag: 'This is plastic too — is it hard?'
If the child says metal must be shiny or silver, show the dull grey spoon.
Reinforce test-minded answers: 'Good — you said let's pour water and see. That's how we find out.'
activities.rationale: Documented KS1 misconceptions include judging a property from appearance, over-generalising one example to a whole material, and using property words loosely apart from observation. Setting up cases where looks mislead and providing physical counterexamples lets children experience that properties must be tested. Letting the surprising result do the teaching can be more persuasive than correction alone, though a single demonstration shows these particular cases rather than proving a universal rule.
sourceClaims: Documented KS1 misconceptions: judging property from appearance (clear plastic vs glass), all-plastic-is-hard / all-metal-is-silver, loose use of property words apart from observation.
learnerActions: Look at a shiny-looking scrap of satin fabric (checked beforehand to make sure water soaks through it) and a dull, matt plastic bag. Before pouring anything, predict which would keep a small toy dry if you wrapped it, and say WHY.

Pour the same small splash of water over each wrapped toy and watch: with the pre-checked fabric, water soaks through the smart-looking shiny material and the toy gets wet, while water runs off the dull plastic and the toy inside stays dry.
Compare your prediction with what happened and say which property word fits each material now.
Explore counterexamples: feel a soft plastic bag (soft but waterproof), handle a dull grey metal spoon (metal but not shiny), and check something rough that is also absorbent.
activities.intendedInsight: Appearance can mislead, and one material comes in many forms — so a property belongs to the tested object, not to how it looks or to the material 'in general'.

constraints: The tap-to-reveal naming scene and the sort/match activities build or check vocabulary; they assert properties and cannot show the actual test, so they must not replace hands-on (or realistically simulated) testing of real material behaviour.

Recognition and sorting formats verify whether words are secure; they do not elicit the child independently conducting a test or describing an observation, which the test-bench and predict-then-pour activities require.

Use property words tied to an observation: insist that describing means saying the word AND what was seen (e.g. 'waterproof — the water rolled off'), to avoid loose interchangeable use of 'strong/hard/stiff'.

Treat stretchy/stiff and bendy/not bendy as two distinct contrasts: stretching pulls a material longer; bending curves or folds it, changing its shape. Do not merge stretchy and bendy into one property, and do not define bendy as 'stays bent' — a bendy material may still spring back.
A material comes in many forms (soft plastic, dull metal); teach properties as belonging to the tested object, not to the material category as a whole.
Keep distinct properties separate: soft is not the same as absorbent, shiny is not the same as transparent — provide counter-cases so each property is judged independently.
For transparency tests, shine a torch AT the material and observe the beam that lands beyond it; never ask a child to look at a bright light source through a material or toward the sun.

Where real materials are available they give tactile evidence a screen simulation cannot; treat any on-screen test bench as a model of the real investigation, not a replacement where hands-on work is possible.

Simulated 'auto-fill the property word after a test' interactions are optional ways to make the mechanism concrete; the required learning is that the child observes a response and names it, not any particular interface.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Two of the three cited sources (NGSS 2-PS1-1 and the STEM Learning misconceptions page) are marked verified:false in the source row; claims attributed to them should be treated as unconfirmed pending re-check.

The original row asserted that a 2D interactive is 'ideal' and that dialogue/3D formats 'add nothing' or cannot teach this. These were catalog fit rankings, not established pedagogical facts, and have been removed/softened: a fixed image or a sort can still support learning, and tactile real-material work remains valuable alongside any screen model.

The predict-then-pour setup assumes a shiny paper towel soaks through and a dull plastic bag stays dry; this depends on the specific materials used. Verify the actual items behave as described before relying on the 'appearance misleads' effect.

The claim that an on-screen 'live recompute' is 'exactly what turns a describing word into an observed fact' overstates a single medium's necessity; retained only as a design idea, not as evidence of comparative efficacy.

The DfE non-statutory list treats 'stretchy/stiff' and 'bendy/not bendy' as separate pairs; the distinct contrasts are preserved, and the earlier 'stays bent / springs back' characterisation of bendy vs stretchy has been corrected to 'bending changes shape / stretching lengthens' because return-behaviour does not define either property.

assess.poeTask: Hold up a shiny paper towel and a dull plastic bag. Before pouring anything, ask the child to PREDICT which will keep a small toy dry and to say WHY. Record the reason. Then pour the same splash of water over each: the 'smart-looking' shiny paper soaks through, the dull plastic stays dry. The reason given BEFORE pouring is the diagnostic part — an appearance-based prediction ('the shiny smooth one') exposes judging-by-looks; a test-minded child says 'I'm not sure yet, let's pour water on and see'.
probeDeeper: You said it's soft — is soft the same as good at soaking up water? Show me something soft that water runs straight off.
Here's a soft squashy plastic bag — so is ALL plastic hard?
This spoon is dull grey — can metal be dull instead of shiny?
How could you check if something is really rough, using your hands with your eyes shut?
assess.correctAnswer: Chooses the plastic bag (waterproof), uses the property word 'waterproof', and proposes a TEST — pour or drip water and see whether it soaks through — rather than judging by looks. Recognises that 'soft' and 'absorbent' are different properties.

errorPatterns.pattern: Judges a property from appearance rather than testing it — 'it looks smooth and shiny so it must be waterproof'.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Introduce a simple fair test (drip the same amount of water on each, watch for soak-through) so a property becomes something observed, not guessed; let the surprise result do the teaching.
errorPatterns.distractor: The shiny smooth one — it looks like it would keep water off.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Names a material as waterproof/absorbent from looks alone and cannot suggest how to check.

errorPatterns.pattern: Over-generalises a property to a whole material — 'all plastic is hard', 'all metal is shiny/silver' — from one example.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Hand over counterexamples (a soft plastic bag, a dull grey spoon) and let the child feel that one material comes in many forms; a property belongs to THIS object, tested, not to the material as a whole.
errorPatterns.distractor: All plastic is hard, so the plastic one can't be the soft bendy one.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Denies that soft plastic or dull metal can exist; predicts a plastic bag must be hard.

errorPatterns.pattern: Collapses distinct properties into one — assumes soft things must also be absorbent, or shiny things must repel water — treating properties as a single good/bad scale.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Line up counter-cases: a soft plastic bag (soft but waterproof), a rough dry sponge (rough but absorbent) so each property varies independently.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Reasons 'it's soft so it'll soak up water' or 'it's shiny so water runs off' without separating the properties.

responseLevels.gap: Uses a describing word as a like/dislike ('it's nice', 'it's good') or judges purely by appearance; cannot suggest any way to check a property.
responseLevels.full: Describes with the correct property word, treats a property as a behaviour to TEST, keeps distinct properties apart, and can give a counterexample (soft-but-not-absorbent, dull metal).
responseLevels.partial: Uses several property words correctly for obvious cases and picks a sensible material, but still judges from looks, over-generalises (all plastic hard), or blurs confusable properties together.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Show a shiny paper towel and a dull grey plastic bag. Say: 'One of these would make a good umbrella and one wouldn't. Which would keep you dry — and how could we FIND OUT if it's really waterproof, instead of just guessing?' Then: 'You said this one is soft — is everything soft also good at soaking up water? Show me something soft that water runs straight off.'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The two items are set up so appearance MISLEADS (the shiny paper looks smart but soaks; the dull bag looks unremarkable but is waterproof). A child who judges by looks picks the shiny one or asserts without a test; a child with the concept treats a property as a behaviour you check and keeps distinct properties (waterproof vs soft vs shiny) apart.
